_about: Passages restating the NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge statement 'Flame in Freefall', indexed so the assistant can answer context questions.

passages.title: Why flames differ in microgravity
passages.text: In microgravity there is no buoyancy, so hot gases do not rise. Instead of a flickering teardrop, a candle flame becomes a blue sphere that relies on diffusion for its oxygen. Air flow is therefore important for flammability in microgravity.

passages.title: NASA fire-safety strategy
passages.text: NASA's spacecraft fire safety work focuses on prevention, detection and suppression. Prevention comes from controlling ignition sources and selecting materials, which depends on understanding flammability limits. Flammability depends strongly on oxygen concentration, and air flow also matters in microgravity. Solid materials such as fabrics and plastics were studied in BASS, BASS-II and Saffire-I, -II and -III. Fire detection was tested through SAME and SAME-R. Suppression was studied in FLEX by diluting the chamber atmosphere with carbon dioxide and helium.

passages.title: Moon base oxygen and pressure
passages.text: Spacesuits are filled with 100% oxygen at only 4.3 psi, while Earth's sea-level pressure is 14.7 psi. To shorten oxygen pre-breathing before moonwalks, Moon bases and pressurized rovers are expected to use a pressure and oxygen level between the two. The oxygen concentration on the Moon will likely be 30% or greater at a pressure of 10.2 psi or less: more than a 40% increase over Earth's air, making materials much more flammable.

passages.title: Highest-oxygen microgravity tests
passages.text: The microgravity tests with the highest oxygen concentrations were in ACME's Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G): an oxygen-nitrogen mixture of up to 85% oxygen flowed from a spherical burner into a chamber of nitrogen and fuel gas, creating an inside-out flame.

passages.title: Partial gravity
passages.text: PSI holds no partial-gravity combustion data yet; it is expected from the Lunar-g Combustion Investigation (LUCI) and the Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2) experiment. ACME's E-FIELD Flames mimicked partial gravity using an electric field acting on the ions in flames. Microgravity and normal-gravity results could bound what happens at intermediate gravity such as on the Moon and Mars.

passages.title: Shared hardware
passages.text: The six ACME experiments burned gaseous fuels with the same modular ACME hardware in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). FLEX, FLEX-2 and the Cool Flames Investigation burned liquid droplets in the Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA). BASS, BASS-II, SPICE and SLICE used the Microgravity Science Glovebox with the fan-driven flow duct built for SPICE.

passages.title: Other relevant investigations
passages.text: An instrument used for smoke detection in SAME and SAME-R was used to detect dust in DAFT and DAFT-2. Although it burned gaseous fuels, the ACME Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) studied the flammability of materials in still atmospheres as a function of material properties.

passages.title: Scope and Earth applications
passages.text: Rocket and propellant fires are outside the scope of PSI, because combustion at rocket-engine speeds is effectively independent of gravity. PSI data also applies on Earth: fine-water-mist extinguishers developed for the ISS have Earth uses, and NASA technology improved smoke detection and firefighter gear such as protective clothing and air tanks.

passages.title: Real spacecraft fires
passages.text: A smoke alarm went off during the Artemis II mission. Apollo 13 suffered an oxygen tank explosion on the way to the Moon. A crew survived a fire aboard the Mir space station caused by an oxygen generator failure. In 1967 the Apollo 1 crew died in a pre-launch test when fire erupted in their oxygen-filled spacecraft.
